# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization reduces rendering load in blocky voxel meshes by reconstructing geometry from triangles and removing faces adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of hidden geometry [S1, unofficial]. It differs from its siblings by operating on the local topological connectivity of the voxel grid to determine face visibility during mesh assembly, rather than relying on camera-relative backface culling, multi-view projection masks, or opacity thresholds.

## Shared principles
The core mechanism relies on the observation that a voxel (typically a cube) has 6 faces, but only those adjacent to empty space (or a different material class) are visible. Naively rendering all faces results in significant overdraw and vertex count inflation [S1, unofficial].

The fundamental algorithm for a uniform cube block is:
1.  **Neighbor Check:** For each voxel at position $P$, iterate through its 6 adjacent positions $P + \mathbf{n}$, where $\mathbf{n}$ is the normal vector of the face being checked [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Visibility Determination:**
    *   Check if a solid voxel exists at $P_{neighbor}$ using the occupied positions set [S1, unofficial].
    *   If a neighbor exists, the face between $P$ and $P_{neighbor}$ is internal and culled [S1, unofficial].
    *   If no neighbor exists, the face is exposed and added to the mesh [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Mesh Assembly:** Combine the meshes of all individual cubes into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' to optimize implementation [S1, unofficial].

For non-uniform or complex shapes, the principle extends to checking specific sub-face coverage or material properties (opacity, transparency) against neighbors [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
A dynamic meshing technique that maintains the visibility of voxel chunk faces by toggling shared geometry state during block insertion or removal, rather than regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from its parent by integrating the face visibility state directly into the block data structure's bit fields, allowing for $O(1)$ local updates instead of global reconstruction. It differs from siblings like [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by relying on explicit neighbor occupancy checks within a fixed-size chunk rather than pre-computed coverage masks.

### [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md)
This method defines a trait-based configuration system that decouples voxel geometry definition from mesh generation logic. It solves the problem of rigid, switch-case-heavy meshing by allowing each block type to declare its own shape, transparency culling behavior, and lighting properties. Unlike the parent method which assumes uniform cube geometry, this approach supports complex shapes (ramps, fluids) and fine-grained transparency control (merged vs. unmerged).

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
Face Coverage Mask Culling is a method for removing hidden faces of partial voxel shapes (such as stairs, slabs, or custom geometries) by representing face coverage as a bit mask. It solves the problem where a boolean "solid/empty" flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. Unlike sibling methods that rely on coarse block visibility or vertex packing, this method operates at the sub-face granularity, allowing precise culling of geometry that is occluded by neighbors while preserving exposed portions of the same face.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management is a dynamic mesh generation and update strategy for voxel terrain that combines face culling with compact vertex storage and incremental buffer updates. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and draw call overhead in voxel rendering by packing vertex attributes into two 32-bit integers and managing mesh topology changes (addition/removal of blocks) through local face interaction logic. It sets itself apart from static meshing methods by supporting real-time incremental updates via a free-list vertex allocator, and from pure geometry shaders by performing all topology calculations on the CPU.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
This method optimizes voxel mesh rendering by rejecting faces that are either occluded by adjacent voxels (internal faces) or oriented away from the camera (backfaces). It distinguishes itself from standard neighbor-check culling by performing visibility tests in projection space to determine front/back orientation, while using a compact bitmask to track internal occlusion, allowing for efficient geometry shader-based culling.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
Block Visibility Culling determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering based on the camera's position and rotation, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the camera has not moved significantly or changed its primary viewing direction. Unlike sibling methods that operate at the fine-grained face level within a block [6723-voxel-face-visibility-check.md], this method operates at the coarse block level, using camera-relative coordinates to cull entire blocks or specific faces based on surface orientation relative to the player. It builds on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by adding camera-relative visibility checks.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
A fast display method for direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It differs from sibling methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) which operate on mesh primitives after assembly; Sobierajski's method operates on the voxel grid directly, projecting voxels to the image plane to avoid holes and using viewing-direction-based culling to reduce the list size before rendering.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
Mask Projection Culling is a visibility-based mesh filtering technique that removes vertices and faces not consistently observed across multiple camera poses by projecting 3D points into camera space and comparing their depth against rendered depth maps or binary masks. It differs from neighbor-based face culling (e.g., [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)) by relying on external camera viewpoints rather than local voxel topology, and from simple back-face culling by using explicit depth/mask validation rather than geometric normals alone.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method culls mesh geometry by comparing projected vertex depths against reference depth maps rendered from multiple camera poses, classifying points as seen, unseen, or forecast to remove artifacts from unbounded Gaussian splatting reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) which rely on voxel neighbor occupancy, by using explicit multi-view visibility constraints derived from camera projections rather than local topological checks.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization for blocky voxel meshes that reduces the number of vertices sent to the GPU by skipping the rendering of voxel faces that are adjacent to existing neighboring voxels. It solves the problem of naively rendering all 6 faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors. It differs from its siblings by performing a direct per-voxel neighbor check during mesh assembly to determine face visibility, rather than using coverage masks, backface culling, or opacity-based thresholds.

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
Opacity-based mesh culling reduces the complexity of polygonal mesh representations of volumetric scenes by discarding geometric primitives that contribute negligible visual information. It solves the problem of excessive mesh count and storage overhead in neural radiance field (NeRF) or similar implicit-to-explicit conversions. Unlike sibling methods that rely on voxel occupancy or spatial connectivity [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md), this method evaluates the optical depth (opacity) of individual triangles or faces against a threshold, retaining only those that significantly affect the final image.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
From-region visibility preprocessing is a technique that precomputes which parts of a 3D scene are visible from specific viewing regions to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of expensive per-frame visibility determination for large datasets by shifting the computational load to an offline phase. Unlike sibling methods that rely on axis-aligned voxel occupancy checks [923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md] or simple backface culling [4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md], this approach handles complex geometry and occluder fusion, though it incurs significant preprocessing overhead.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The algorithm resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterates through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`). For each block, it determines if it is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and sets the corresponding flag in the bitmask. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The first pass (opaque) generates faces for opaque blocks. If the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air), generating opaque faces between air and transparent blocks. Otherwise, it tests for non-air blocks. The second pass (transparent) tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks. It generates faces for all transparent blocks touching air, but does not add faces between transparent and solid blocks (since solid blocks already have those faces). It filters out solid block types during the transparent pass: before constructing the AO value and adding the block type to the hashmap, it checks if in the transparent pass; if so, it ignores any block types that are not transparent [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The technique originated as a solution to the inefficiency of instantiating full cube models for every voxel. Early implementations noted that rendering all 6 sides of a cube (12 triangles) when only 1 side is visible leads to unnecessary rendering load [S1, unofficial]. The method was implemented by creating a class that reconstructs cubes from triangles and checks for solid neighbors to determine which sides to render [S1, unofficial]. To further optimize, meshes of all cubes were combined into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial]. This approach was notably used in early voxel engines like Minecraft, where chunk sizes were limited by vertex count restrictions (e.g., ~65,000 vertices in Unity) [S1, unofficial].
